questions.title: AWS Regions, Availability Zones and Global Infrastructure
questions.question: What are AWS Regions and Availability Zones and why do they matter for backend architecture?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Region: geographic area with multiple AZs (e.g., us-east-1, ap-south-1)
- Availability Zone: one or more isolated data centers within a region, separate power/networking
- High availability: deploy across multiple AZs — failure of one AZ doesn't bring down the service
- Latency: choose a region close to your users to minimize network round trips
- Data residency: some regulations require data to stay in specific regions (GDPR → EU regions)
- Services that are regional: EC2, RDS, ECS; global services: IAM, CloudFront, Route53

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
A Region is a geographic location — like Mumbai (ap-south-1) or Virginia (us-east-1) — that contains multiple Availability Zones. An Availability Zone is essentially one or more physically separate data centers within the region, with independent power, cooling, and networking. The physical separation means a failure in one AZ — a power outage, flood, or hardware failure — doesn't affect the others.

For backend architecture, AZs are the foundation of high availability. You deploy your application in at least two AZs behind a load balancer. If one AZ has a problem, the load balancer routes all traffic to instances in the healthy AZ. Your database runs in Multi-AZ mode, where the standby is in a different AZ and automatic failover happens in minutes.

Region choice matters for latency and compliance. If your users are in India, running in ap-south-1 Mumbai gives 10-20ms latency versus 200ms from us-east-1. If you're handling EU user data, GDPR may require you to run in eu-west or eu-central regions.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## AWS Global Structure

```
AWS Cloud
├── Region: us-east-1 (N. Virginia)
│   ├── AZ: us-east-1a (Data Center Cluster A)
│   ├── AZ: us-east-1b (Data Center Cluster B)
│   └── AZ: us-east-1c (Data Center Cluster C)
├── Region: ap-south-1 (Mumbai)
│   ├── AZ: ap-south-1a
│   ├── AZ: ap-south-1b
│   └── AZ: ap-south-1c
└── Region: eu-west-1 (Ireland)
    ├── AZ: eu-west-1a
    └── ...
```

## Multi-AZ Architecture (Java Backend)

```
                    Internet
                       │
               [Route 53 DNS]
                       │
            [Application Load Balancer]
                 /            \
    AZ-1a                         AZ-1b
    [EC2/ECS App Server]    [EC2/ECS App Server]
           │                        │
    [RDS Primary]  ←──────→  [RDS Standby]
    (AZ-1a)        sync repl   (AZ-1b)
```

## Key Regional vs Global Services

| Service | Scope |
|---------|-------|
| EC2, ECS, RDS | Regional (choose AZ) |
| S3 | Regional (globally accessible) |
| IAM | Global |
| Route 53 | Global |
| CloudFront | Global (edge locations) |
| VPC | Regional |

## Spring Boot: Configuring AWS SDK Region

```java
@Configuration
public class AwsConfig {
    @Value("${aws.region:ap-south-1}")
    private String region;

    @Bean
    public S3Client s3Client() {
        return S3Client.builder()
            .region(Region.of(region))
            .credentialsProvider(DefaultCredentialsProvider.create())
            .build();
    }
}
```

speakable_v2.cap: If you're handling EU user data, GDPR may require you to run in eu-west or eu-central regions.

questions.title: VPC, Subnets and Security Groups
questions.question: How does AWS VPC networking work and how do you secure a Java backend with subnets and security groups?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- VPC: isolated virtual network with your own IP address range (CIDR block)
- Public subnet: has route to Internet Gateway — for load balancers, NAT gateways
- Private subnet: no direct internet route — for application servers and databases
- Security Group: stateful firewall rules at the instance level — allow inbound/outbound traffic
- NACL: stateless subnet-level firewall — less common, but provides subnet-level isolation
- NAT Gateway: lets private subnet instances initiate outbound internet traffic (for package downloads, API calls)
- Principle: database in private subnet, only accessible from app security group

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
A VPC is your private isolated network within AWS. You define a CIDR block — the range of IP addresses — and divide it into subnets. Public subnets have a route to the Internet Gateway and are for resources that need to be directly accessible from the internet, like your load balancer. Private subnets have no direct internet route and are for your application servers and databases.

The recommended Java backend architecture is to put your load balancer in the public subnet, your application servers in a private subnet, and your database in a separate private subnet. The application servers can reach the internet for outbound calls through a NAT Gateway in the public subnet, but no inbound traffic from the internet can reach them directly.

Security Groups act as stateful firewalls per resource. Stateful means if you allow inbound traffic on port 8080, the response traffic is automatically allowed without a separate outbound rule. A best practice is chaining security groups — the database security group only allows inbound on port 5432 from the application security group's ID, not from a CIDR range. This means only your actual app instances can talk to the database.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Recommended VPC Layout

```
VPC: 10.0.0.0/16
├── Public Subnet AZ-a: 10.0.1.0/24
│   ├── Application Load Balancer
│   └── NAT Gateway
├── Public Subnet AZ-b: 10.0.2.0/24
│   └── Application Load Balancer (multi-AZ)
├── Private Subnet AZ-a: 10.0.10.0/24
│   └── ECS/EC2 App Servers
├── Private Subnet AZ-b: 10.0.11.0/24
│   └── ECS/EC2 App Servers
├── DB Subnet AZ-a: 10.0.20.0/24
│   └── RDS Primary
└── DB Subnet AZ-b: 10.0.21.0/24
    └── RDS Standby
```

## Security Group Chain

```
ALB Security Group:
  Inbound: 443 from 0.0.0.0/0 (internet)
  Outbound: 8080 to App-SG

App Security Group:
  Inbound: 8080 from ALB-SG only
  Outbound: 5432 to DB-SG, 443 to 0.0.0.0/0 (via NAT)

DB Security Group:
  Inbound: 5432 from App-SG only  ← only app can reach DB
  Outbound: (not needed for RDS)
```

## Spring Boot: Use IAM Roles, Not Hardcoded Credentials

```yaml
# application.yml — no AWS keys here!
spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://${RDS_ENDPOINT}:5432/appdb
    # RDS_ENDPOINT injected via environment variable or Secrets Manager
```

```java
// AWS SDK automatically uses EC2/ECS instance role credentials
// No access keys needed when running on AWS with proper IAM role
S3Client s3 = S3Client.builder()
    .credentialsProvider(DefaultCredentialsProvider.create())
    // DefaultCredentialsProvider checks: env vars → system props → EC2 instance metadata
    .build();
```

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: This means only your actual app instances can talk to the database.

questions.title: EC2 Instance Types and Auto Scaling
questions.question: How do you choose EC2 instance types and set up auto scaling for a Java Spring Boot application?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Instance families: t-series (burstable, cheap), m-series (general purpose), c-series (compute), r-series (memory)
- For Java apps: m5/m6i general purpose or c5/c6i for CPU-intensive workloads
- JVM needs memory: heap + metaspace + thread stacks — don't size EC2 just for heap
- Auto Scaling Group (ASG): automatically add/remove instances based on metrics
- Scaling policies: target tracking (maintain 60% CPU), step scaling, scheduled scaling
- Lifecycle hooks: run custom actions before instance terminates (graceful shutdown)
- Use launch templates, not launch configurations (newer, more features)

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
For a Java Spring Boot backend, I typically start with m-series instances — general purpose with a balanced CPU to memory ratio. Java applications need more memory than their configured heap because the JVM also uses memory for metaspace, thread stacks, and native libraries. A rule of thumb is to provision 2-3x your max heap size as total instance memory. So if you configure -Xmx2g, use an instance with at least 4-6GB RAM.

T-series burstable instances are cheaper but unreliable for consistent workloads. They earn CPU credits when idle and spend them during bursts. A Java backend that has steady consistent load will run out of CPU credits and be throttled, causing unpredictable latency spikes. Use t-series only for dev/test environments.

Auto Scaling Groups are how you handle variable load. You define minimum, desired, and maximum instance counts, and policies that trigger scaling. Target tracking is the simplest — tell it to keep average CPU at 60% and it adds or removes instances automatically. For Spring Boot, add a lifecycle hook to give instances 30-60 seconds to finish in-flight requests before termination.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Instance Type Selection

| Family | Best For | Java Use Case |
|--------|----------|---------------|
| t3/t4g | Dev/Test, low traffic | Non-production only |
| m5/m6i | General purpose | Standard Spring Boot apps |
| c5/c6i | Compute-intensive | High-throughput APIs, batch |
| r5/r6i | Memory-intensive | Large heap JVM, Elasticsearch |
| g4/g5 | GPU | ML inference |

## JVM Memory Sizing

```
EC2 Memory: 8GB
├── JVM Heap (-Xmx):    4GB
├── Metaspace:         512MB
├── Thread stacks:     256MB (100 threads × 256KB)
├── DirectByteBuffer:  512MB (Netty, NIO)
├── OS overhead:      ~1GB
└── Free buffer:      ~768MB

JVM flags for 8GB instance:
-Xms2g -Xmx4g -XX:MetaspaceSize=256m -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=512m
```

## Auto Scaling with Graceful Shutdown

```java
// Spring Boot: graceful shutdown (built-in since 2.3)
// application.yml
server:
  shutdown: graceful
spring:
  lifecycle:
    timeout-per-shutdown-phase: 30s  # wait up to 30s for in-flight requests
```

```bash
# ASG Lifecycle Hook — give container 60s to drain
# In User Data or lifecycle hook action:
aws autoscaling complete-lifecycle-action \
  --lifecycle-action-result CONTINUE \
  --lifecycle-hook-name app-termination-hook \
  --auto-scaling-group-name my-asg \
  --instance-id $INSTANCE_ID
```

## CloudWatch Scaling Policy

```json
{
  "PolicyType": "TargetTrackingScaling",
  "TargetTrackingConfiguration": {
    "PredefinedMetricSpecification": {
      "PredefinedMetricType": "ASGAverageCPUUtilization"
    },
    "TargetValue": 60.0,
    "ScaleInCooldown": 300,
    "ScaleOutCooldown": 60
  }
}
```

questions.title: AWS Load Balancers — ALB vs NLB
questions.question: What is the difference between ALB and NLB in AWS and when do you use each for a Java backend?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- ALB (Application Load Balancer): Layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS) — routes by path, host, headers; supports WebSocket, gRPC
- NLB (Network Load Balancer): Layer 4 (TCP/UDP) — ultra-low latency, preserves source IP, handles millions of connections
- ALB target types: EC2 instances, ECS tasks, Lambda, IP addresses
- Path-based routing: /api/* → backend service, /static/* → S3 or frontend service
- ALB sticky sessions: route same client to same backend (use with caution)
- Health checks: ALB checks HTTP endpoint; NLB checks TCP connection
- NLB: use for gaming, IoT, financial trading — when latency matters more than HTTP features

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
For most Java Spring Boot backends, the Application Load Balancer is the right choice. It operates at HTTP level, so you can make routing decisions based on URL paths, host headers, or HTTP headers. This enables you to put multiple microservices behind one ALB and route based on path — /api/orders routes to the order service, /api/inventory routes to the inventory service.

ALB also integrates natively with AWS Certificate Manager for HTTPS termination, with Cognito for authentication, and with WAF for security rules. The backend receives plain HTTP, which reduces the complexity in your Spring Boot application.

NLB is for when you need extreme low latency or need to preserve the client's source IP. It operates at TCP level and doesn't parse HTTP at all — packets are just forwarded. You'd use NLB for WebSocket connections that need very high throughput, or for non-HTTP protocols. A common pattern is NLB in front of ALB when you need a static IP address, since ALB doesn't have static IPs but NLB does.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## ALB Path-Based Routing

```
ALB: api.example.com
├── /api/orders/*    → Target Group: order-service (ECS tasks)
├── /api/products/*  → Target Group: product-service (ECS tasks)
├── /api/auth/*      → Target Group: auth-service (ECS tasks)
└── /* (default)     → Target Group: frontend (EC2 or S3 redirect)
```

## ALB vs NLB Comparison

| Feature | ALB | NLB |
|---------|-----|-----|
| Layer | 7 (HTTP/HTTPS) | 4 (TCP/UDP) |
| Routing | Path, host, headers | IP+Port |
| Latency | ~1-5ms | <1ms |
| Static IP | No (DNS only) | Yes |
| SSL Termination | Yes | Yes (passthrough option) |
| WebSocket | Yes | Yes |
| gRPC | Yes | Yes |
| Source IP Preservation | Via X-Forwarded-For header | Native |

## Health Check Configuration

```
# Spring Boot Actuator health endpoint for ALB health checks
GET /actuator/health → 200 OK = healthy, 5xx = unhealthy
```

```yaml
# application.yml
management:
  endpoints:
    web:
      base-path: /actuator
  endpoint:
    health:
      show-details: when-authorized

# ALB Health Check settings:
# Path: /actuator/health
# Interval: 30s
# Healthy threshold: 2 (consecutive 200s)
# Unhealthy threshold: 3 (consecutive failures)
# Timeout: 5s
```

## Spring Boot: Get Client IP Behind ALB

```java
@GetMapping("/api/info")
public String getClientInfo(HttpServletRequest request) {
    // ALB adds X-Forwarded-For with original client IP
    String clientIp = request.getHeader("X-Forwarded-For");
    if (clientIp == null) clientIp = request.getRemoteAddr();
    return clientIp;
}
```

speakable_v2.hook: For most Java Spring Boot backends, the Application Load Balancer is the right choice.
speakable_v2.cap: A common pattern is NLB in front of ALB when you need a static IP address, since ALB doesn't have static IPs but NLB does.

questions.title: Monitoring with CloudWatch
questions.question: How do you set up effective monitoring and alerting for a Java Spring Boot application using CloudWatch?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- CloudWatch Metrics: time-series data — EC2 CPU, memory (with CloudWatch agent), custom app metrics
- CloudWatch Logs: centralized log aggregation from EC2/ECS — filter and alarm on log patterns
- CloudWatch Alarms: trigger SNS notifications or Auto Scaling actions based on metric thresholds
- Metric filters: extract numeric values from log lines (error count, p99 latency)
- CloudWatch Container Insights: ECS/EKS container-level metrics
- Spring Boot Micrometer → CloudWatch metrics publisher
- Dashboard: combine multiple metrics for at-a-glance operational view

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
CloudWatch is AWS's monitoring and observability service. For a Spring Boot application, I set up three layers of monitoring. First, infrastructure metrics — EC2 CPU, memory (requires the CloudWatch agent), network, and disk. Second, application metrics via Micrometer, which is Spring Boot's metrics facade. Third, log monitoring via CloudWatch Logs where I create metric filters to count errors and trigger alarms.

Micrometer with the CloudWatch metrics registry lets you publish custom application metrics — JVM heap usage, database connection pool utilization, custom business metrics like orders per minute — directly to CloudWatch. You then build dashboards combining infrastructure and application metrics for a complete operational view.

For alerting, I set CloudWatch Alarms on the most actionable metrics. CPU alarm for scaling, 5xx error rate alarm for application problems, database connection exhaustion alarm for capacity issues. Alarms trigger SNS notifications which can email the team, trigger a PagerDuty incident, or send a Slack message.

questions.title: AWS Secrets Manager and Parameter Store
questions.question: How do you securely manage database credentials and API keys in a Spring Boot application on AWS?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Never hardcode credentials in code or application.yml committed to git
- AWS Secrets Manager: stores and rotates secrets (DB passwords, API keys) — costs per secret
- AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store: free tier available, SSM GetParameter in code
- Secrets Manager rotation: automatic credential rotation with Lambda — no restart needed
- Spring Cloud AWS: Spring-native integration for reading Secrets Manager and Parameter Store
- IAM role on EC2/ECS: grants application permission to read specific secrets only
- At rest encryption: Secrets Manager uses KMS by default

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The fundamental rule is that credentials should never appear in source code or in configuration files that get committed to a repository. AWS provides two services for this: Secrets Manager for sensitive secrets that need rotation like database passwords, and Parameter Store for configuration values and less sensitive parameters.

Secrets Manager is the better choice for database credentials because it integrates with RDS to automatically rotate passwords on a schedule. When a rotation happens, Secrets Manager updates the secret value and you read the latest value from the SDK — your application doesn't need to restart. This is hugely valuable for security because you can rotate credentials regularly without any downtime.

For Spring Boot, Spring Cloud AWS provides a bootstrap integration that reads from Secrets Manager or Parameter Store at startup and makes the values available as Spring properties. Your application.yml references ${db.password} and Spring resolves it from the secret store. The application gets the IAM permission to read those specific secrets through its EC2 or ECS task role — no access keys needed.

questions.title: AWS SQS and SNS for Async Communication
questions.question: How do you use AWS SQS and SNS for asynchronous messaging in a Java Spring Boot application?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- SQS: message queue — point-to-point, messages stored until consumed, auto-retry
- SNS: pub/sub topic — one publisher, many subscribers (SQS, Lambda, HTTP, email)
- Standard queue: at-least-once delivery, best-effort ordering
- FIFO queue: exactly-once processing, strict ordering, lower throughput
- Dead Letter Queue (DLQ): messages that fail after max retries go here for investigation
- Visibility timeout: message hidden from other consumers while being processed
- Fan-out pattern: SNS topic → multiple SQS queues for different services

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
SQS is a message queue for point-to-point async communication. One producer sends a message, one consumer picks it up, processes it, and deletes it. If processing fails, the message becomes visible again after the visibility timeout and another consumer can pick it up and retry. After too many failures, it goes to the Dead Letter Queue for investigation. This pattern decouples services and provides natural buffering against load spikes.

SNS is a pub/sub system. You publish one message to a topic and SNS fan-outs to all subscribers — SQS queues, Lambda functions, HTTP endpoints, email. This is how you implement the fan-out pattern: an order placed event publishes to an SNS topic, and the inventory service, notification service, and analytics service each have their own SQS queue subscribed to that topic.

For Spring Boot, Spring Cloud AWS provides @SqsListener annotations that work similarly to @KafkaListener — you annotate a method and the framework handles polling, message parsing, and deletion on successful processing.

questions.question: What are the core AWS services a Java/Spring Boot developer should know, and what does each do?
questions.title: Core AWS Services Overview for Java Developers
questions.direct_answer: A Java/Spring Boot developer should be familiar with EC2 (virtual machines), S3 (object storage), RDS (managed relational databases), Lambda (serverless functions), SQS (message queues), and SNS (pub/sub notifications). Each solves a different infrastructure concern and maps directly to common backend patterns.

interviewer_intent.testing: Breadth of AWS knowledge and ability to map services to use cases
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Listing services without explaining when or why you would use them
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain how services integrate — e.g., Lambda triggered by SQS, or Spring Boot reading from S3 on startup

sections.title: Why Service Integration Matters More Than Service Memorization
sections.content:
The trap in this question is treating it as a memorization exercise — listing 15 AWS services with one-line descriptions. Interviewers have heard that answer hundreds of times. What they actually want is evidence that you understand **how services compose** to solve backend problems.

A Spring Boot backend on AWS operates across three layers that mirror what you already do locally: **compute** (where the JVM runs), **data** (where state lives), and **integration** (how services communicate). Each layer has a default choice and an escalation path. The default is simpler and cheaper; the escalation handles specific requirements the default can't meet.

The connective pattern across all three layers is IAM — every AWS SDK call your Spring Boot app makes is authenticated via the task role or instance profile. Credentials rotate automatically without touching your code. Understanding this credential flow matters more than knowing what CloudFront does, because it determines how every service interaction actually works at runtime.

sections.title: The Service Map: Default vs Escalation for Each Backend Concern
sections.content:
| Backend Concern | Default Choice | Escalation Trigger | Escalation |
|---|---|---|---|
| HTTP microservice | **ECS Fargate** — containers without EC2 | Need event-driven, sub-second billing | **Lambda** (with SnapStart for Java) |
| Relational data | **RDS PostgreSQL** — managed, familiar JDBC | Need 5× throughput or global replication | **Aurora** |
| NoSQL / key-value | **DynamoDB** — single-digit ms at any scale | Need SQL flexibility, ad-hoc queries | Stay on RDS |
| Message queue | **SQS** — durable, pull-based, at-least-once | Need fan-out to multiple consumers | **SNS → SQS** pattern |
| Event routing | **SNS** — simple pub/sub | Need content-based routing, schema registry | **EventBridge** |
| File storage | **S3** — object storage, presigned URLs | Need block storage for EC2 | EBS |
| Caching | **ElastiCache Redis** — managed, VPC-native | Need global replication | ElastiCache Global Datastore |
| Secrets | **Secrets Manager** — auto-rotation, $0.40/secret/mo | Need cheap config storage (non-secret) | **Parameter Store** (free tier) |
| Monitoring | **CloudWatch** — metrics + logs + alarms | Need APM-level tracing | **X-Ray** or third-party |

sections.title: How Services Compose: The Patterns That Signal Real Experience
sections.content:
The interview differentiator is explaining **integration patterns**, not individual services. Here are the compositions that come up in real production architectures:

**SNS → SQS fanout**: A single order-created event publishes to an SNS topic. Three SQS queues subscribe — one for inventory, one for billing, one for email notifications. Each consumer processes independently at its own pace. If the billing service goes down, its SQS queue buffers messages until it recovers. This pattern decouples publishers from consumers and provides durability that SNS alone doesn't offer.

**Lambda triggered by SQS**: An SQS queue receives image-processing requests. Lambda polls the queue, scales automatically based on queue depth, and processes images in parallel. Spring Cloud Function makes the Lambda handler a plain `Function<SQSEvent, Void>` bean — your business logic stays portable between Lambda and ECS.

**S3 presigned URLs via Spring Boot**: Instead of routing file uploads through your Spring Boot server (consuming bandwidth and memory), generate a presigned PUT URL and return it to the client. The client uploads directly to S3. Your server only handles URL generation — milliseconds instead of minutes.

**ECS + Secrets Manager + RDS in a VPC**: The ECS task definition references Secrets Manager ARNs for the database password. The task role grants `secretsmanager:GetSecretValue`. The ECS service and RDS instance share private subnets in the same VPC. No credentials in code, no public database endpoints, no manual secret rotation.

Spring Cloud AWS simplifies all of these: `@SqsListener` for SQS consumers, `S3Template` for object operations, and property source integration for Secrets Manager values as Spring properties.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **ECS Fargate: containerized compute, no EC2 management** — push a Docker image, declare CPU/memory; AWS schedules placement; no AMI patching or capacity planning for the underlying host
- **RDS/Aurora for relational data; DynamoDB for key-value at scale** — Spring Data JPA works with both RDS and Aurora; DynamoDB requires the DynamoDB-enhanced client or Spring Data DynamoDB
- **S3 for object storage, not relational data** — cheapest durable blob storage; use for files, images, exports, and large payloads; not a database
- **SQS for point-to-point; SNS for fan-out** — SQS keeps messages until a consumer processes them; SNS broadcasts to all subscribers simultaneously; EventBridge adds content-based routing rules
- **Lambda for event-driven, infrequent work** — zero cost when idle; cold starts matter for latency-sensitive paths; use SnapStart or provisioned concurrency to eliminate cold starts for Java

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
AWS for Java backend work organizes around three layers — compute where the JVM runs, data storage, and the messaging and integration services that connect them. Knowing which service belongs in which layer makes it easy to pick the right one for each job.

**Compute — where the application runs**
- ECS Fargate runs Docker containers without managing EC2 instances — which means you define CPU and memory, push a container image, and AWS schedules and runs it; no patching, no capacity planning for VMs
- EC2 is the right choice when you need control over the instance type, GPU access, or specific AMIs; for most Spring Boot services, Fargate is simpler
- Lambda runs event-driven functions billed per invocation — which means zero cost when idle; the trade-off is cold starts and a 15-minute execution limit

**Data storage**
- RDS and Aurora handle relational workloads with full JDBC and Hibernate support; Aurora PostgreSQL adds auto-scaling storage and replicas with no operational overhead
- S3 stores object data — files, images, backups, large JSON payloads; not a database, but the cheapest and most durable way to store blobs
- DynamoDB is a fully managed NoSQL key-value store; useful when you need single-digit millisecond latency at any scale without managing schema migrations

**Messaging and integration**
- SQS decouples producer and consumer services with a durable queue — which means the producer doesn't need the consumer to be running at the same time
- SNS fans out one event to multiple subscribers — one publish, many consumers via HTTP, email, or SQS subscriptions
- EventBridge routes events from AWS services or custom sources to targets based on content-based rules

For a standard Spring Boot microservice: Fargate for compute, RDS for data, SQS for async communication — these three cover 80% of what backend services need on AWS.

sections.title: Why Fargate Eliminates the Hardest Part of Container Deployment
sections.content:
Before Fargate, deploying containers on AWS meant managing an ECS cluster backed by EC2 instances — choosing instance types, tuning capacity providers, patching AMIs, and handling instance draining during deployments. Fargate removes all of that: you define **CPU and memory for your container**, and AWS places, scales, and patches the underlying infrastructure.

The deployment flow has five concrete steps, but the part that trips most developers up isn't the deployment itself — it's the **IAM role distinction** between what ECS needs to run your container (execution role) and what your Spring Boot code needs to access AWS services (task role). Confusing these two produces identical-looking permission errors that are hard to debug without understanding the model.

The other production concern unique to Java is **resource sizing**. A Spring Boot app with typical dependencies needs at least 512 MB of memory for the JVM heap plus container overhead. Under-sizing causes OOMKilled restarts that look like application bugs.

sections.title: Containerize With a Multi-Stage Build That Keeps Images Small
sections.content:
A multi-stage Dockerfile separates the build environment (JDK, Maven, source code) from the runtime environment (JRE only, final JAR). This typically cuts the image from ~800 MB to ~200 MB, which directly reduces pull time during deployments and cold starts.

```dockerfile
FROM maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-21 AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY pom.xml .
RUN mvn dependency:go-offline  # cached layer unless pom changes
COPY src ./src
RUN mvn package -DskipTests

FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app/target/*.jar app.jar
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0", "-jar", "app.jar"]
```

The `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0` flag is critical for containers. Without it, the JVM calculates heap size based on the host machine's memory (potentially 64 GB on the underlying Fargate host), not the container's memory limit. With it, the JVM uses 75% of the container's allocated memory, leaving headroom for non-heap memory (metaspace, thread stacks, native buffers).

After building, push to ECR — AWS's private container registry that integrates with ECS and IAM.

```bash
aws ecr get-login-password --region us-east-1 | \
  docker login --username AWS --password-stdin 123456789.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com
docker build -t my-spring-app . && \
docker tag my-spring-app:latest 123456789.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/my-spring-app:latest && \
docker push 123456789.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/my-spring-app:latest
```

sections.title: The Task Definition: Two Roles, Health Checks, and Secrets
sections.content:
The task definition is the deployment descriptor — it specifies the container image, resource limits, IAM roles, secrets, and health check configuration. Getting the IAM roles right here prevents the most common Fargate permission errors.

The **execution role** is what ECS uses to pull your image from ECR and send container logs to CloudWatch. The **task role** is what your Spring Boot application assumes at runtime to access S3, SQS, Secrets Manager, and other services. These are separate IAM roles with separate policies.

```json
{
  "family": "order-service",
  "networkMode": "awsvpc",
  "requiresCompatibilities": ["FARGATE"],
  "cpu": "512",
  "memory": "1024",
  "executionRoleArn": "arn:aws:iam::123456789:role/ecsTaskExecutionRole",
  "taskRoleArn": "arn:aws:iam::123456789:role/order-service-task-role",
  "containerDefinitions": [{
    "name": "order-service",
    "image": "123456789.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/order-service:v1.2",
    "portMappings": [{"containerPort": 8080}],
    "secrets": [{
      "name": "DB_PASSWORD",
      "valueFrom": "arn:aws:secretsmanager:us-east-1:123456789:secret:order-db-password"
    }],
    "healthCheck": {
      "command": ["CMD-SHELL", "curl -f http://localhost:8080/actuator/health || exit 1"],
      "interval": 30,
      "retries": 3,
      "startPeriod": 60
    }
  }]
}
```

The `startPeriod: 60` gives Spring Boot 60 seconds to start before health checks begin — without this, a slow-starting JVM fails health checks during startup and ECS kills the task before it's ready. The `secrets` block pulls values from Secrets Manager at container start, injecting them as environment variables without exposing them in the task definition or image.

sections.title: Service Creation, ALB, and Auto Scaling for Production Traffic
sections.content:
The ECS service maintains a desired count of running tasks, replaces unhealthy ones, and integrates with the Application Load Balancer for traffic routing. The ALB performs its own health checks against `/actuator/health` — only tasks that pass both the container health check and ALB health check receive traffic.

```bash
aws ecs create-service \
  --cluster production \
  --service-name order-service \
  --task-definition order-service:3 \
  --desired-count 2 \
  --launch-type FARGATE \
  --network-configuration "awsvpcConfiguration={\
    subnets=[subnet-private-1,subnet-private-2],\
    securityGroups=[sg-app],\
    assignPublicIp=DISABLED}" \
  --load-balancers "targetGroupArn=arn:aws:...,containerName=order-service,containerPort=8080"
```

Notice `assignPublicIp=DISABLED` — the tasks run in private subnets and receive traffic only through the ALB. This is the standard production topology: ALB in public subnets, application tasks in private subnets, RDS in isolated subnets.

For auto-scaling, ECS Service Auto Scaling adjusts the task count based on CloudWatch metrics. Target tracking on CPU utilization is the simplest policy — it adds tasks when average CPU exceeds the target and removes them when it drops.

```bash
aws application-autoscaling put-scaling-policy \
  --service-namespace ecs \
  --resource-id service/production/order-service \
  --scalable-dimension ecs:service:DesiredCount \
  --policy-name cpu-70-target \
  --policy-type TargetTrackingScaling \
  --target-tracking-scaling-policy-configuration \
    '{"TargetValue":70,"PredefinedMetricSpecification":{"PredefinedMetricType":"ECSServiceAverageCPUUtilization"}}'
```

For zero-downtime deployments, configure the service with a **blue/green deployment** via CodeDeploy — it spins up new tasks with the new image, routes test traffic to them, then shifts production traffic only after the new tasks pass health checks.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Multi-stage Dockerfile keeps the image small** — build in a JDK stage, copy only the JAR to a JRE final stage; distroless or alpine base; smaller image = faster pulls and smaller attack surface
- **ECR in the same region as ECS avoids transfer costs** — image pulls from ECR to ECS in the same region are free and fast; cross-region pulls incur data transfer charges
- **Task definition: IAM task role, not instance role** — assign an IAM role to the task definition, not the EC2 instance; this scopes permissions to the specific service, not the entire host
- **ALB health check on `/actuator/health`** — ECS deregisters tasks that fail health checks; configure the check path, interval, and unhealthy threshold before deploying
- **Rolling deployment with `minimumHealthyPercent: 50`** — old tasks stay running until new tasks pass health checks; `maximumPercent: 200` allows running twice the desired count during the rollout

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Deploying a Spring Boot application to ECS Fargate follows four stages: containerize, push to a registry, define the task, and create the service. Each stage has one common mistake that causes deployment failures.

**Containerize — multi-stage Dockerfile**
- A multi-stage Dockerfile builds the JAR in a Maven or Gradle stage and copies only the JAR into the final image — which means the final container doesn't include the JDK build tools, keeping the image small and reducing the attack surface
- Use a distroless or slim JRE base image for the final stage: `FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine` gives a minimal runtime

**Push to ECR**
- Create an ECR repository with `aws ecr create-repository --repository-name my-service`; authenticate with `aws ecr get-login-password | docker login`; tag and push the image
- ECR stores images in the same region as ECS, which means image pulls are fast and don't incur cross-region data transfer costs

**Task definition — CPU, memory, environment**
- The ECS task definition specifies the container image, CPU units, memory, port mappings, IAM task role, and environment variables — environment variables for database URLs and feature flags go here, secrets come from Secrets Manager via the `secrets` field
- Set `essential: true` so ECS restarts the task if the container exits

**Service — load balancing and health checks**
- The ECS service maintains a desired count of running tasks, registers them with an ALB target group, and replaces unhealthy tasks automatically
- Configure the ALB health check to call Spring Boot's `/actuator/health` endpoint — ECS marks tasks unhealthy if the health check fails, replacing them before taking traffic

For zero-downtime deployments: use the `ECS (Rolling update)` deployment type with `minimumHealthyPercent: 50` and `maximumPercent: 200` so old tasks remain until new ones pass health checks.

sections.title: The Cold Start Problem That Made Java on Lambda Impractical — and What Fixed It
sections.content:
Java on Lambda had a reputation problem: cold starts took **8-15 seconds** for a typical Spring Boot application because Lambda had to initialize the JVM, load all classes, and create the full Spring application context on every cold invocation. For HTTP APIs behind API Gateway, this meant the first request after an idle period took 10+ seconds — unacceptable for user-facing services.

Two technologies fundamentally changed this equation. **AWS Lambda SnapStart** (available for Java 11, 17, and 21) takes a snapshot of the initialized JVM after the Spring context is fully loaded and restores it on cold start — reducing initialization from seconds to **~200ms**. **GraalVM native images** compiled with Spring Native eliminate the JVM entirely, starting in **<100ms** with a fraction of the memory.

Spring Cloud Function provides the abstraction layer: you write a standard `Function<I, O>` bean, and the `spring-cloud-function-adapter-aws` module wraps it as a Lambda handler. Your business logic stays portable — the same function can run on Lambda, on ECS as an HTTP endpoint, or as a Pub/Sub consumer, without code changes.

sections.title: Writing the Function Bean: Business Logic That Doesn't Know About Lambda
SnapStart: How JVM Checkpointing Eliminates Cold Starts
sections.content:
SnapStart works by running your Lambda function's initialization code **once during deployment**, taking a memory snapshot (using the CRaC — Coordinated Restore at Checkpoint — framework), and storing it encrypted. On cold start, Lambda restores the snapshot instead of re-initializing, cutting startup from ~10 seconds to ~200ms.

Enabling SnapStart requires one configuration change — no code modifications. In your SAM template or CloudFormation:

```yaml
Resources:
  OrderProcessorFunction:
    Type: AWS::Serverless::Function
    Properties:
      Handler: org.springframework.cloud.function.adapter.aws.FunctionInvoker::handleRequest
      Runtime: java21
      SnapStart:
        ApplyOn: PublishedVersions  # enables snapshot on publish
      MemorySize: 512
      Timeout: 30
      Environment:
        Variables:
          SPRING_CLOUD_FUNCTION_DEFINITION: processOrder
```

The critical detail is that SnapStart snapshots happen at **publish time**, not at every deployment. You must publish a new version (`aws lambda publish-version`) for the snapshot to be created. Using `$LATEST` bypasses SnapStart entirely — a common mistake that leaves cold starts unimproved.

There's one catch with SnapStart: any state that's unique per invocation — database connections, random number generators, temporary credentials — must be refreshed after restore. Spring Cloud Function handles most of this automatically, but if you have custom initialization code that opens connections or generates UUIDs during startup, wrap it in a `@PostConstruct` with CRaC lifecycle awareness.

For teams that can't use SnapStart (older runtimes, or needing even faster starts), GraalVM native compilation with `spring-boot-maven-plugin` and the `native` profile produces a standalone binary that starts in <100ms with ~50 MB of memory — versus 200-500 MB for a JVM Lambda.

sections.title: SQS Batch Processing: The Pattern That Makes Lambda Cost-Effective
Key Points
sections.content:
- **`Function<I, O>` bean is Lambda-agnostic** — Spring Cloud Function wraps it with the Lambda adapter; the function itself has no AWS SDK imports or Lambda-specific types
- **Cold start is the primary Java Lambda challenge** — 3-10s JVM + Spring startup; mitigate with SnapStart (snapshot the initialized JVM), provisioned concurrency (pre-warm instances), or GraalVM native image
- **Memory setting controls CPU allocation** — Lambda allocates CPU proportionally; a CPU-bound function at 256MB runs 4x slower than at 1024MB; profile first to find the memory/cost optimum
- **SnapStart reduces Java cold start to under 1 second** — available for Java 11+ on Corretto runtime; AWS takes a snapshot after initialization and restores it on invocation; no code changes required
- **Use Lambda for event-driven, infrequent work; Fargate for sustained traffic** — at constant high volume, Fargate's fixed cost beats per-invocation Lambda pricing; Lambda excels when traffic is bursty or zero at times

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Spring Cloud Function lets you write a standard Java `Function<I, O>` bean and deploy it to AWS Lambda with minimal Lambda-specific code. The framework handles the adapter layer between Lambda's handler interface and your function.

**Writing the function**
- Define a `@Bean` of type `Function<InputType, OutputType>` — Spring Cloud Function discovers it by name and routes Lambda invocations to it; the function knows nothing about Lambda's event envelope
- For HTTP API Gateway events: the `aws-serverless-java-container` adapter or the Spring Cloud Function AWS adapter converts the API Gateway request into an `HttpServletRequest` before calling your function

**Cold starts — the Java Lambda problem**
- The JVM's class loading and Spring's ApplicationContext startup cause cold starts of 3-10 seconds on the first invocation, which means the first request after a period of inactivity is slow for users
- Two mitigations: Lambda SnapStart (available for Java 11+ on Corretto) snapshots the initialized JVM and restores it, reducing cold start to under 1 second; provisioned concurrency pre-warms a fixed number of instances at all times (costs money even when idle)
- GraalVM native image compiled with Spring Native eliminates JVM startup entirely — cold starts under 100ms, but compilation takes longer and some reflection-heavy libraries need configuration

**Memory and performance**
- Lambda CPU is allocated proportionally to memory — 1024MB gives roughly 0.5 vCPU; 3008MB gives approximately 1.5 vCPU; which means CPU-bound functions benefit from higher memory settings even if they don't use the extra RAM
- Profile the function with `AWS X-Ray` to see where initialization time is spent — often Spring auto-configuration for features the function doesn't need

Use Lambda for: event-driven processing (S3 events, SQS triggers, scheduled jobs), lightweight API endpoints behind API Gateway. Avoid Lambda for: long-running batch jobs, anything requiring stateful connections, or services that receive constant traffic where ECS/Fargate is more cost-effective.

sections.title: The Architecture Mistake: Routing File Bytes Through Your Application Server
sections.content:
The naive approach to file uploads is: client sends a multipart POST to your Spring Boot controller, the controller reads the file into memory, then uploads it to S3. For a 10 MB profile picture, this works. For a 500 MB video or 10,000 concurrent uploads, your application server becomes a **file proxy** — consuming heap memory, network bandwidth, and Tomcat threads for data that's just passing through.

The production pattern is **presigned URLs**: your Spring Boot server generates a time-limited URL that authorizes the client to upload or download directly to/from S3. The server handles only the URL generation (milliseconds), and the client handles the data transfer (seconds to minutes). Your application never touches the file bytes.

This distinction — proxying bytes vs. generating presigned URLs — is what interviewers are testing. Both approaches use the same S3 SDK, but the presigned URL pattern demonstrates an understanding of how production systems handle file operations at scale.

sections.title: Streaming Uploads and Downloads: When Your Server Must Handle Bytes
Presigned URLs: The Pattern That Scales File Operations Without Server Cost
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Presigned URL for uploads/downloads skips the server** — client uploads directly to S3; server generates a time-limited signed URL; eliminates server bandwidth, memory, and connection usage for file transfer
- **`S3Client.putObject` with streaming avoids loading files into memory** — use `RequestBody.fromInputStream()` with a content length; never buffer large files in a byte array before uploading
- **`S3Template` from Spring Cloud AWS simplifies common operations** — wraps SDK client with Spring idioms; inherits IAM credential resolution from the task or instance role automatically
- **Never make buckets public; use presigned or CloudFront signed URLs** — presigned URLs expire after a configured duration (15 min to 7 days); CloudFront signed URLs allow longer expiry with CDN distribution
- **Enable versioning and SSE on user-upload buckets** — versioning recovers accidental overwrites; SSE-S3 (or SSE-KMS for key management compliance) encrypts all objects at rest

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
S3 integration in Spring Boot comes down to one architectural decision: does your server proxy the file bytes through itself, or does it generate a presigned URL and let the client upload or download directly?

**Presigned URLs — the right default**
- A presigned URL is a time-limited S3 URL that grants the holder permission to read or write a specific object — your server generates it with `S3Presigner.presignPutObject()` and returns it to the client, which then uploads directly to S3
- This is the correct approach for uploads because the file never passes through your server — which means your server doesn't consume bandwidth, memory, or connection slots for large uploads; S3 handles the inbound data transfer directly

**Direct upload via the server — when necessary**
- If you need to validate, transform, or virus-scan the file before storing it, the server must receive the bytes — use `S3Client.putObject(PutObjectRequest, RequestBody.fromInputStream(stream, length))` with a streaming approach to avoid loading the entire file into memory
- Set `Content-Type` and `ContentDisposition` on the PutObjectRequest so S3 serves the file with the correct headers when downloaded

**Using Spring Cloud AWS**
- `spring-cloud-aws-starter-s3` provides `S3Template` which wraps the SDK client with Spring idioms — `s3Template.upload(bucket, key, inputStream)` for uploads, `s3Template.download(bucket, key)` returns a `Resource`
- Inject `S3Template` as a bean; Spring Cloud AWS handles credential resolution from the IAM task role automatically in ECS

**Access control**
- Never make buckets public; use presigned URLs for time-limited access; for long-term sharing, generate CloudFront signed URLs through a distribution in front of S3

sections.title: The Decision Most Teams Overthink: 90% of Java Services Should Use RDS
sections.content:
The temptation is to choose DynamoDB because it's "more scalable" or Aurora because it's "faster than standard Postgres." But both come with trade-offs that most applications never benefit from. **RDS PostgreSQL** with standard JDBC, Hibernate, and Spring Data JPA is the correct default for the vast majority of Java backend services — it's familiar, flexible, cheap, and handles thousands of TPS on a modest instance.

The decision becomes interesting only when you hit specific requirements that RDS can't meet. Aurora addresses relational scale and availability: up to 5× Postgres throughput, 6-way storage replication, and global databases for cross-region reads. DynamoDB addresses a fundamentally different access pattern: single-digit millisecond key-value lookups at any scale, but **only if you design your data model around partition keys and access patterns upfront**.

The common mistake this question tests for is choosing DynamoDB because it sounds impressive, then discovering weeks later that your reporting queries, join operations, or ad-hoc filters require scanning the entire table — something DynamoDB does poorly and expensively.

sections.title: The Trade-Off Matrix: What Each Database Does Best and Worst
sections.content:
| Dimension | RDS PostgreSQL | Aurora PostgreSQL | DynamoDB |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Data model** | Relational (SQL) | Relational (SQL) | Key-value / Document |
| **Query flexibility** | ✅ Ad-hoc SQL, JOINs, CTEs | ✅ Same as Postgres | ❌ Partition key + sort key only |
| **Spring Data** | ✅ JPA / Hibernate native | ✅ Same as RDS | ⚠️ Enhanced Client, no JPA |
| **Throughput** | ~5K TPS standard | ~25K TPS (5× RDS) | Millions TPS (on-demand) |
| **Read latency** | 2-5ms | 1-3ms | <10ms consistent |
| **Storage** | Max 64 TB | Auto-scales to 128 TB | Unlimited |
| **Multi-region** | ❌ Read replicas only | ✅ Global Database | ✅ Global Tables |
| **Serverless option** | ❌ | ✅ Aurora Serverless v2 | ✅ On-demand mode |
| **Cost (starting)** | ~$30/mo (db.t3.micro) | ~$60/mo (db.t3.medium min) | ~$1.25/million writes |
| **Schema changes** | Flyway/Liquibase + downtime risk | Same | Schema-free |
| **Best for** | Standard CRUD, reports, joins | High-perf relational at scale | Session store, catalog, IoT |

sections.title: The Decision Framework: Three Questions That Pick Your Database
sections.content:
**Question 1: Do you need SQL flexibility — JOINs, aggregations, ad-hoc queries?**
If yes, you're relational. Choose between RDS and Aurora.

**Question 2: Do you need more throughput than a large RDS instance provides, or cross-region active reads?**
If yes, choose **Aurora**. Aurora's storage engine replicates data 6 ways across 3 AZs, handles up to 15 read replicas with <20ms replica lag, and offers Global Database for cross-region reads. **Aurora Serverless v2** is the right choice for variable-traffic workloads — it scales from 0.5 ACUs ($43/month equivalent) to hundreds of ACUs automatically, so you don't pay for peak capacity during off-hours.

If no, stay on **RDS**. It's cheaper, simpler, and fully compatible with every Postgres tool — `pg_dump`, `pgAdmin`, PostGIS, Flyway. Don't pay the Aurora premium for capabilities you don't use.

**Question 3: Is your access pattern entirely key-value — get item by ID, query by partition key + sort key, no JOINs?**
If yes, **DynamoDB** delivers single-digit millisecond reads at any scale with zero operational overhead. Session stores, shopping carts, IoT telemetry, and API rate limiting are ideal DynamoDB use cases.

The critical requirement: you must **design your data model around your access patterns before writing any code**. DynamoDB has no query optimizer — if you need a query pattern you didn't plan for, you either add a Global Secondary Index (expensive at scale) or scan the entire table (even more expensive).

**DynamoDB Streams** adds event-driven capability: every write to the table produces a stream record that can trigger a Lambda function. This enables patterns like: write to DynamoDB (fast, consistent), then asynchronously update a search index, send a notification, or replicate to another region. The Spring Cloud AWS DynamoDB module provides a `DynamoDbTemplate` and an enhanced client that maps Java records to DynamoDB items with type-safe annotations.

My decision rule: **start with RDS PostgreSQL. Move to Aurora when you outgrow it. Use DynamoDB only for specific access patterns that are genuinely key-value.** Never choose DynamoDB for a workload where you might need ad-hoc queries later.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **RDS for standard JDBC/JPA workloads** — PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle; Spring Data JPA works without code changes; scales vertically; right for most transactional Spring Boot services
- **Aurora PostgreSQL for high availability and storage auto-scaling** — six-way replication in three AZs; no storage provisioning; read replicas add capacity without additional storage cost; Aurora Serverless v2 scales compute granularly
- **DynamoDB for key-value access at any scale** — horizontally partitioned; single-digit millisecond latency; no SQL; queries are limited to partition key and sort key; use GSIs for alternate access patterns
- **DynamoDB requires schema design upfront** — access patterns must be known at design time; adding a new access pattern often requires a GSI or data migration; unlike RDS where SQL adapts easily to new queries
- **Aurora Serverless v2 for variable workloads** — scales between minimum and maximum ACU (Aurora Capacity Units); cost-effective for dev, staging, or services with unpredictable traffic spikes

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
AWS offers three primary managed database options for Java backend services — RDS, Aurora, and DynamoDB — and the right choice depends on whether you need relational semantics, operational simplicity, or scale-first design.

**RDS — standard relational, full Hibernate support**
- RDS runs managed PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle, or SQL Server — which means Spring Data JPA, Hibernate, and JDBC work without any code changes; you choose the engine version and instance size, and AWS handles backups, patching, and failover
- The limitation: RDS scales vertically — when you need more capacity, you move to a larger instance class; there's a ceiling, and the migration requires a brief downtime

**Aurora — relational with cloud-native storage**
- Aurora separates compute from storage — the storage layer replicates across six copies in three Availability Zones automatically, which means a storage node failure doesn't cause data loss and read replicas can be added with no additional storage cost
- Aurora PostgreSQL is compatible with PostgreSQL, so Spring Data JPA and Hibernate work identically; the difference is Aurora's storage auto-scales from 10GB to 128TB and multi-master configurations allow write scaling
- Aurora Serverless v2 scales compute capacity in fine-grained increments between a minimum and maximum — which means you pay for what you use and idle services scale close to zero

**DynamoDB — key-value, single-digit millisecond at any scale**
- DynamoDB is a NoSQL key-value and document store that handles any amount of traffic by partitioning data horizontally — you define a partition key and optionally a sort key; queries are limited to the key structure
- Spring Data DynamoDB or the Enhanced DynamoDB Client maps Java objects to DynamoDB items; there's no JPA, no SQL, and no joins — cross-entity queries require pre-computed indexes (GSI) or denormalized data
- Choose DynamoDB when: workloads are simple key lookups or range scans on the primary key, traffic is highly variable, or the dataset is too large for a relational engine

questions.question: What is the difference between SQS, SNS, and EventBridge, and when do you use each?
questions.title: SQS vs SNS vs EventBridge — Messaging Service Comparison
questions.direct_answer: SQS is a pull-based durable queue for point-to-point messaging between services. SNS is a push-based pub/sub fanout service. EventBridge is an event bus with rich content-based routing, schema registry, and integrations with AWS services and SaaS providers. They are often combined: SNS fans out to SQS queues, or EventBridge routes events to SQS/Lambda targets.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of distributed messaging patterns and trade-offs
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using SNS for durable message delivery — SNS does not guarantee delivery if a subscriber is down; combine with SQS for durability
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Describe the SNS → SQS fanout pattern and when EventBridge's content-based routing removes the need for application-level conditional logic

sections.title: Three Services That Look Similar Until You Lose Messages in Production
sections.content:
These three services occupy different positions on the messaging spectrum, and the mistake that causes production incidents is using the wrong one. **SQS** is a durable queue — messages persist until a consumer processes and deletes them. If the consumer is down, messages wait. **SNS** is fire-and-forget pub/sub — it pushes messages to subscribers immediately, but if a subscriber is down, that message is gone (unless the subscriber is an SQS queue). **EventBridge** is a smart event router — it examines event content and routes based on rules, enabling event-driven architectures without application-level routing logic.

The critical distinction most developers miss: **SNS alone does not provide durable delivery**. If you publish an event to an SNS topic and the subscribing HTTP endpoint is down, that event is lost after retry exhaustion. This is why the **SNS → SQS fanout pattern** exists: SNS fans out to SQS queues, and each queue provides durability for its consumer independently.

In a Spring Boot context, `@SqsListener` handles SQS consumption with automatic acknowledgement, `SnsTemplate` or the SDK handles publishing to SNS, and EventBridge integrates through the SDK's `PutEvents` API.

sections.title: The Messaging Decision Matrix
sections.content:
| Dimension | SQS | SNS | EventBridge |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Model** | Pull-based queue | Push-based pub/sub | Event bus + rules |
| **Durability** | ✅ Messages persist up to 14 days | ❌ Lost if subscriber is down | ✅ Archive + replay up to 14 days |
| **Delivery** | At-least-once (standard) / Exactly-once (FIFO) | At-least-once to active subscribers | At-least-once |
| **Consumers** | 1 per message (standard queue) | Many subscribers per topic | Many rules per bus |
| **Ordering** | ✅ FIFO queues guarantee order | ❌ No ordering | ❌ No ordering |
| **Content routing** | ❌ All messages go to same queue | ✅ Filter policies on attributes | ✅ Rich event pattern matching |
| **Dead letter** | ✅ DLQ after N failures | ❌ | ✅ DLQ per rule target |
| **Max message size** | 256 KB (up to 2 GB via S3) | 256 KB | 256 KB |
| **Spring integration** | `@SqsListener` annotation | `SnsTemplate` | SDK `PutEvents` |
| **Cost** | $0.40/million requests | $0.50/million publishes | $1.00/million events |
| **Best for** | Work queues, task processing | Notifications, fanout | Cross-service event routing |

sections.title: The Three Patterns That Cover 90% of Messaging Use Cases
sections.content:
**Pattern 1: SQS as a work queue** (point-to-point). One producer, one consumer. Messages are durable — if the consumer crashes, messages wait in the queue. Use this for background job processing, order fulfillment, email sending. Spring Cloud AWS's `@SqsListener` makes consumption trivial.

```java
@SqsListener("order-processing-queue")
public void processOrder(OrderEvent event) {
    orderService.fulfill(event); // auto-ack on success, requeue on exception
}
```

The visibility timeout determines how long SQS waits before redelivering a message to another consumer. Set it to at least 6× your average processing time to prevent duplicate processing during slow operations. Dead-letter queues capture messages that fail after N retries.

**Pattern 2: SNS → SQS fanout** (one event, many consumers). An order-created event needs to reach inventory, billing, and notification services independently. Publish to an SNS topic, subscribe each service's SQS queue to that topic. Each queue buffers messages independently — if billing is down, inventory and notifications still process.

SNS filter policies can route based on message attributes: `{"eventType": ["ORDER_CREATED"]}` on the billing subscription ensures it only receives order events, not shipment events published to the same topic.

**Pattern 3: EventBridge for cross-service routing** (content-based). When routing logic goes beyond simple attribute filtering — you need to match on nested JSON fields, numeric ranges, or prefix patterns — EventBridge's rule engine replaces application-level conditional logic. An event rule can match `{"detail": {"orderTotal": [{"numeric": [">", 1000]}]}}` to route high-value orders to a fraud detection Lambda.

EventBridge also integrates with SaaS sources (Stripe, Auth0, Datadog), AWS service events (EC2 state changes, ECS task stops), and has a schema registry that generates Java DTOs from event schemas. The cost is higher ($1/million vs $0.40/million for SQS), justified when the routing complexity would otherwise require custom code.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **SQS: durable queue, at-least-once delivery** — message stays until the consumer deletes it after processing; visibility timeout allows retry if consumer crashes; FIFO queues add ordering and exactly-once semantics
- **SNS: push-based fan-out, no persistence** — one publish reaches all subscribers simultaneously; if a subscriber is unavailable, the message is lost unless the subscriber is an SQS queue
- **EventBridge: content-based routing with rules** — route events to different targets based on event content; content-based filtering without custom code; supports AWS service events and custom event buses
- **SNS + SQS fan-out is the most common pattern** — SNS publishes; multiple SQS queues subscribe; each consumer gets independent durability and retry without knowing about the others
- **SQS dead-letter queue (DLQ) captures failed messages** — configure `maxReceiveCount` and a DLQ; messages that fail processing N times move to the DLQ for inspection without blocking the main queue

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
SQS, SNS, and EventBridge are three different AWS messaging primitives — each designed for a different integration pattern. Choosing the wrong one for the job is a common architecture mistake.

**SQS — durable queue, point-to-point**
- SQS holds messages until a consumer explicitly deletes them after processing — which means if the consumer crashes during processing, the message becomes visible again after the visibility timeout and can be reprocessed by another consumer
- Standard queues provide at-least-once delivery; FIFO queues provide exactly-once delivery with ordering within a message group, at lower throughput
- Use SQS when: one service produces work items and one service processes them; you need durability and retry on consumer failure; you don't need immediate fan-out to multiple consumers

**SNS — push-based fan-out**
- SNS publishes one message to all registered subscribers simultaneously — SQS queues, Lambda functions, HTTP endpoints, email; which means one event published by a service can trigger multiple independent consumers without the producer knowing about them
- SNS does not persist messages — if a subscriber is unavailable when the publish happens, the message is lost (unless the subscriber is an SQS queue, which buffers for it)
- Use SNS when: one event must trigger multiple independent downstream workflows; fan-out is the pattern

**EventBridge — content-based routing**
- EventBridge routes events from AWS services, custom applications, or SaaS partners to targets based on event content rules — `source = "orders-service" AND detail.status = "PLACED"` routes to one Lambda; `detail.status = "CANCELLED"` to another
- EventBridge is the right choice when routing logic is complex, events come from multiple sources, or you want to decouple producers from consumers with schema-validated events via the Event Schema Registry

**Common pattern: SNS + SQS fan-out**
- Producer publishes to SNS; multiple SQS queues subscribe — each consumer has its own queue, buffered and retried independently; this combines fan-out (SNS) with durability and retry (SQS)

questions.question: How does IAM work in AWS, and what is the least privilege principle?
questions.title: IAM Roles and Policies — Least Privilege Principle
questions.direct_answer: IAM (Identity and Access Management) controls who can do what on which AWS resources. Least privilege means granting only the permissions required to perform a specific task — nothing more. Spring Boot apps should use IAM roles attached to their compute (EC2 instance profile, ECS task role) rather than hardcoded access keys.

interviewer_intent.testing: Security awareness and understanding of AWS authentication/authorisation model
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using IAM user access keys in application code or environment variables instead of IAM roles, and using wildcard (*) actions in policies

sections.title: The Mistake That Turns a Minor Vulnerability Into a Full Account Compromise
sections.content:
Every AWS API call — whether from the console, CLI, or your Spring Boot application — is authenticated and authorized by IAM. The authentication part determines **who** is making the call. The authorization part determines **whether they're allowed to**. Getting this wrong doesn't just break functionality — it determines the blast radius when something goes wrong.

The most dangerous IAM anti-pattern in Java applications is using **long-lived access keys** — `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` and `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` in environment variables, properties files, or Docker images. These keys never expire, can't be rotated without application changes, and grant whatever permissions are attached to that IAM user. A leaked key (in a Git commit, a log dump, a CI artifact) gives an attacker persistent access until the key is manually revoked.

The solution is **IAM roles attached to compute**: EC2 instance profiles, ECS task roles, Lambda execution roles. The AWS SDK's default credential chain discovers these credentials automatically — no keys in code, no environment variables, and credentials rotate every few hours without any application awareness.

Least privilege means each role has **exactly the permissions needed, on exactly the resources needed, and nothing more**. Not `s3:*` on `*` — but `s3:GetObject` on `arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket/uploads/*`.

sections.title: The Two-Role Model: Execution Role vs Task Role in ECS
Policy Conditions: The Advanced Constraint Most Developers Never Use
Key Points
sections.content:
- **IAM roles over IAM users for compute resources** — roles provide temporary credentials rotated automatically; IAM user access keys are permanent and must be rotated manually; never store access keys in environment variables or code
- **Least privilege: specific actions on specific ARNs** — `s3:PutObject` on `arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket/*` instead of `s3:*` on `*`; scope every permission to the exact resource the service uses
- **ECS task role provides credentials automatically** — the AWS SDK resolves credentials from the ECS metadata endpoint without any configuration; no AWS keys in application.properties
- **IAM conditions narrow permissions further** — `aws:SourceVpc`, `s3:prefix`, and `aws:RequestedRegion` add context-based restrictions that prevent credentials from being used outside expected boundaries
- **IAM Access Analyzer validates policies** — use AWS IAM Access Analyzer to identify overly permissive policies, unused permissions, and external access before deploying to production

IAM controls every API call in AWS — it handles both authentication (proving who you are) and authorization (determining what you're allowed to do). Understanding least-privilege IAM is essential because overly permissive roles are the most common AWS security finding.

**IAM roles vs IAM users**
- An IAM user has permanent credentials (access key + secret); an IAM role is assumed by a resource and provides temporary credentials via STS
- For ECS tasks, Lambda functions, and EC2 instances: always use IAM roles, never IAM users; the platform automatically rotates the temporary credentials, which means you don't store or manage long-lived secrets in the environment

**Least privilege — the principle**
- Least privilege means granting only the exact permissions a service needs and nothing more — which means an ECS task that writes to one S3 bucket should have `s3:PutObject` on that specific bucket ARN, not `s3:*` on `*`
- Over-permissive roles are the single most exploited attack vector in AWS breaches; a compromised task with `s3:*` exposes all your buckets; a compromised task with `s3:PutObject` on one bucket exposes only that

**IAM policy structure**
- Policies have Effect (Allow/Deny), Action (the API operations), Resource (the specific ARN), and optional Condition — `aws:SourceIp`, `aws:RequestedRegion`, and `s3:prefix` are common conditions that narrow access further
- Start with AWS managed policies for common roles (e.g., `AmazonECSTaskExecutionRolePolicy`) and add custom policies for your specific resource ARNs

**In Spring Boot on ECS**
- Assign the IAM task role in the task definition; the AWS SDK automatically calls the ECS metadata endpoint to retrieve temporary credentials — no AWS key configuration in environment variables or application.properties
- Use `@Value("${aws.region}")` from the ECS metadata, not hardcoded; the SDK's DefaultCredentialsProvider chain resolves credentials automatically

sections.title: The Cost-vs-Capability Trade-Off Most Teams Get Wrong
sections.content:
Both services store configuration, both support encryption, and both integrate with Spring Boot through Spring Cloud AWS. The confusion is understandable — they overlap significantly. The difference becomes clear when you ask: **does this value need to rotate automatically, and how much am I willing to pay for that capability?**

Secrets Manager costs **$0.40 per secret per month** plus $0.05 per 10,000 API calls. It provides built-in automatic rotation through Lambda functions — you can rotate an RDS password every 30 days without any application changes. Parameter Store's standard tier is **free** (up to 10,000 parameters), and the advanced tier costs $0.05 per parameter per month.

The practical consequence: if you store 50 configuration values (database URLs, feature flags, timeout settings) in Secrets Manager, you're paying $20/month for capability you don't use. Store them in Parameter Store for free, and keep Secrets Manager for the 5 values that actually need rotation — database passwords, API keys, OAuth client secrets.

sections.title: Spring Cloud AWS Integration: Loading Both Sources as Spring Properties
sections.content:
Spring Cloud AWS provides property source integration for both services, letting you reference secrets and parameters in `application.yml` as standard Spring properties. The separation is clean: Secrets Manager values are prefixed differently from Parameter Store values, and both resolve before the application context initializes.

The configuration uses Spring profiles and a hierarchical path convention. Parameter Store parameters follow a path like `/order-service/prod/db-url`, and Spring Cloud AWS maps the path to Spring property names automatically.

```yaml
# application.yml
spring:
  config:
    import:
      - aws-parameterstore:/order-service/  # loads all params under this prefix
      - aws-secretsmanager:order-db-password  # loads specific secret

# Then reference them as normal properties
spring.datasource.url: ${db-url}  # from Parameter Store
spring.datasource.password: ${order-db-password}  # from Secrets Manager
feature.new-checkout: ${new-checkout-enabled}  # from Parameter Store
```

The hierarchical path convention means `/order-service/prod/db-url` maps to the Spring property `db-url` when the application is running with the `prod` profile. This keeps environment-specific configuration in Parameter Store without any code changes between environments.

For automatic refresh (picking up Parameter Store changes without restart), enable Spring Cloud's `@RefreshScope` on beans that read configuration properties. Secrets Manager values typically require a restart because they're injected during DataSource initialization, but Parameter Store values used for feature flags or timeouts can refresh dynamically.

sections.content:

- **Parameter Store: use for configuration and non-rotating encrypted values** — feature flags, environment config, SecureString for non-rotating sensitive values; free for standard parameters
- **Spring Cloud AWS integrates both as PropertySource** — `@Value("${/myapp/prod/db-password}")` resolves from Parameter Store at startup; `spring-cloud-aws-starter-secretsmanager` does the same for Secrets Manager
- **Never store secrets in environment variables or `application.properties`** — environment variables appear in ECS task definition logs and `ps aux` output; Secrets Manager/Parameter Store keeps them out of the code and config files
- **Secrets Manager costs more but provides rotation** — ~$0.40/secret/month; Parameter Store SecureString costs ~$0.05/parameter/month for advanced tier; use Secrets Manager only when rotation is a requirement

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
AWS Secrets Manager and Systems Manager Parameter Store both securely store configuration, but they serve different purposes — Secrets Manager is for credentials that must rotate; Parameter Store is for configuration that changes infrequently.

**Secrets Manager — for credentials with rotation**
- Secrets Manager stores secrets (database passwords, API keys, OAuth tokens) and can automatically rotate them on a schedule — which means your RDS password rotates every 30 days and the Lambda or ECS task that reads it at runtime gets the current version, without a deployment
- Automatic rotation uses a Lambda function that updates both Secrets Manager and the underlying resource (e.g., the RDS password) atomically; if the update fails, the old secret remains valid

**Parameter Store — for configuration and non-secret values**
- Parameter Store stores both plain-text and encrypted (SecureString) parameters; it's free for standard parameters and supports hierarchical paths — `/myapp/prod/database-url`, `/myapp/prod/feature-flag-enabled`
- SecureString parameters use KMS for encryption and cost the same as Secrets Manager at much lower usage, but without automatic rotation
- Use Parameter Store for: feature flags, environment-specific config, non-rotating encrypted values, and anything you'd otherwise put in a properties file

**Integration with Spring Boot**
- Spring Cloud AWS provides `spring-cloud-aws-starter-secretsmanager` and `spring-cloud-aws-starter-parameter-store` — both integrate as Spring `PropertySource` implementations, which means you reference secrets with `@Value("${my-secret-key}")` and Spring resolves them at startup from AWS
- Cache the resolved values to avoid fetching from AWS on every property access; configure `spring.cloud.aws.secretsmanager.reload.strategy` for runtime rotation pickup without restarts

questions.question: How do you set up a CI/CD pipeline for a Spring Boot application using AWS CodePipeline and CodeBuild?
questions.title: Deploying with AWS CodePipeline and CodeBuild
questions.direct_answer: CodePipeline orchestrates the pipeline stages (source → build → deploy). CodeBuild executes the build — it compiles the Java code, runs tests, builds the Docker image, and pushes it to ECR. The deploy stage updates the ECS service or Elastic Beanstalk environment with the new image. A buildspec.yml file in the repo controls what CodeBuild runs.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not caching Maven/Gradle dependencies in CodeBuild, leading to slow builds that download the internet every time
